disclosure_text: I am 2nd generation Mexican American, my mom was born in Mexico and immigrated to the USA when she was a teenager in the late 1960's.  She came to the USA with a green card with her mom/my grandma.  Her mother got a job as a maid with a family in southern California where she stayed for many years. I feel I have direct connection to the experience of immigrants in seeing how my mom and my grandma were treated.  I also have experience from my own life seeing how Hispanic Americans are treated.
micronarrative: The town hall’s divide mirrors my family’s history. My mom and grandma arrived from Mexico in the late 60’s on green cards but were still treated as second-class citizens—a reality that fuels my anger. Growing up, I was one of few minorities in school, where classmates would mock Mexicans but then say, “You’re not like *those* people,” as if my identity could be compartmentalized. My dad prioritized English over Spanish, teaching me to read with English books and Sesame Street, ensuring I’d “fit in.” I never struggled with English—no accent, fluent vocabulary—but Spanish remained tied to my grandma’s kitchen, a quiet bridge to heritage. Now, seeing crowds shout about “local safety” while others serve tea, I hear echoes of the same dehumanizing rhetoric my family faced. The scenario’s tension isn’t abstract: it’s the same choice I’ve navigated my whole life—code-switching to belong, while carrying a history that resists erasure.

chat_log.content: Reading through that passage — what stands out to you first? Is there something you connect with on a personal level, or something that feels distant?

The first thing that immediately stands out to me is this misguided notion that undocumented immigrants are a danger to the public when in fact the majority are families with children who are coming to this country for a better life.   This is something that feels intensely personal to me because my mom and my grandma came to this country as immigrants from Mexico in the late 60's and even though they came on a green card, they were still treated like they were second class citizens and it angers me to think about that.
How have you personally experienced others perceiving you or your family because of your Mexican heritage?

I grew up in a pretty middle class background.  I was lucky, my dad worked for the county as a health inspector so I was able to have nice things and go to nice schools but I was often one of the few minorities at my school growing up so I always was aware of being different.  I would commonly here people making fun of  mexicans and they would always say things like "you're not  like those other ones that I'm talking about..you're cool", stuff like that but I would still be upset.

This is a great question because my dad make a concerted effort in my house to make sure that he emphasized my learning English as being more important than Spanish.  I spoke Spanish also mostly to my grandma and
Were there moments when learning or using English felt especially challenging, or when your way of communicating was misunderstood by others?

No, I have always been fluent in English, never had an accent..if anything my Spanish was what I really had to work on.  My dad taught me to read  using books in English, I watched sesame street, Mr Rogers etc.  I never had trouble with English and always have had a very good vocab and no accent.
